content_groups.group_title: Q1. What is the definition of labour?

blocks.text: Regular uterine contractions associated with progressive cervical effacement and dilatation, resulting ultimately in delivery of the fetus and placenta.

content_groups.group_title: Q2. How do you know labour is established?

blocks.text: Regular painful contractions associated with progressive cervical change.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What are the three stages of labour?

blocks.text: First stage: onset of established labour to full cervical dilatation. Second stage: full dilatation to birth of the baby. Third stage: birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta and membranes.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What does severe moulding suggest?

blocks.text: Possible difficulty with passage of the fetal head, particularly when associated with poor descent and increasing caput.

content_groups.group_title: Q9. What would make you concerned about obstructed labour?

blocks.text: Failure of descent or cervical progress despite adequate contractions, especially with increasing caput, moulding, malposition, maternal exhaustion or fetal compromise.

content_groups.group_title: Q10. Should every woman in labour have continuous CTG?

blocks.text: No. In uncomplicated low-risk labour, intermittent auscultation may be appropriate. Continuous CTG is used when there are relevant maternal or fetal risk factors or concerns.

items: “How would you assess a woman presenting in labour?”

blocks.text: “I would first introduce myself, confirm her identity, establish gestational age and parity, explain the assessment and obtain consent. I would ask about the onset, frequency and duration of contractions, rupture of membranes, vaginal bleeding, fetal movements, pain and any antenatal complications. I would assess maternal observations and general condition. Abdominal examination would assess uterine size, lie, presentation, position, engagement, contractions and fetal heart rate. If indicated, I would perform a consented vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation and effacement, presentation, position, station, membranes, liquor, caput and moulding. I would then determine whether labour is progressing normally and whether there are any maternal or fetal concerns requiring intervention.”
